common_name: Angel Wing Solomon's Seal (Wide Creamy-Margined Fragrant Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light to half shade; 'Angel Wing' (PP 21,543), a selection by Massachusetts plantsman Roy Herold, is valued for its extra-wide creamy-white leaf margins and red-tinted emerging stems.

directions: 'Angel Wing' bears glossy, arching stems clothed in leaves with an unusually wide, creamy-white margin that gives the foliage a bright, luminous quality even in deep shade, while new stems emerge reddish before aging to green. Small, dangling, white, tubular bells hang beneath the arching stems in late spring. It is a notably vigorous grower for a variegated Solomon's seal, spreading by branching rhizomes to form a broad clump roughly a yard wide within about five years, and tolerates several hours of morning sun as well as fuller shade. Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil, mulch with leaf litter to mimic its native woodland floor, and divide congested clumps in spring once the colony becomes crowded.

common_name: Double Stuff Solomon's Seal (Extra-Wide White-Margined Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; 'Double Stuff' (PP 19,624), discovered by Pennsylvania plantsman Bill Lamack in 1997, carries leaf margins nearly twice the width of the common 'Variegatum' and grows more slowly because of its reduced chlorophyll.

directions: Double Stuff is a slow-growing, heavily variegated selection of fragrant Solomon's seal whose creamy-white leaf margins are nearly double the width of those on the familiar 'Variegatum', giving each red-tinted, 18-inch stalk an unusually bold, bright appearance. Small, dangling, white, bell-shaped flowers appear beneath the arching stems in spring. Because so much of the leaf lacks chlorophyll, the plant increases more slowly than green-leaved or lightly variegated Solomon's seals, making it best suited to a prominent spot in the woodland garden rather than mass groundcover use. Grow in evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled to full shade, and top-dress annually with compost or leaf mold to keep the shallow rhizomes cool and fed.

common_name: Goldilocks Solomon's Seal (Gold-Streaked Fruiting Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light to half shade; 'Goldilocks', a Plant Delights seedling selection out of the cultivar 'Spiral Staircase', bears leaves heavily streaked golden and, unusually for a variegated Solomon's seal, sets a heavy crop of fertile blue fruit.

directions: Goldilocks carries sturdy, 18-inch stalks lined with broad green leaves heavily streaked and marbled golden-yellow, an effect that from a distance reads as soft silvery-gold foliage. It is an especially vigorous grower for a variegated form and, unusual among gold- or white-marked Solomon's seals, produces a heavy crop of dark blue, marble-sized berries each fall, many of which germinate true to the golden variegation. In hot summer climates the gold streaking can fade toward green with the heat, recovering its brighter color as temperatures cool. Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, and allow the rhizomes room to spread into an increasingly showy colony over several seasons.

common_name: Silver Saddle Solomon's Seal (Compact Silver-Ridged Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; 'Silver Saddle', a Juniper Level Botanic Garden/Plant Delights introduction bred from 'Goldilocks' crossed with 'Koryu', is a compact, fast-multiplying selection with dark purple stalks and a raised silvery ridge running down the center of each leaf.

directions: Silver Saddle is a compact hybrid selection of fragrant Solomon's seal, its foot-long arching, dark purple stalks set with medium green leaves each marked by a distinctive raised silver ridge down the center. It multiplies markedly faster than its parent 'Koryu' while staying noticeably more compact, making it useful for smaller shaded borders or containers where larger Solomon's seals would overwhelm the space. Stalks are strung with small, white, tubular bell-shaped flowers in early spring. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, mulching with leaf litter to keep the shallow rhizomes cool, and divide established clumps in spring as the colony fills in.

common_name: Red Legs Solomon's Seal (Large-Leaved Carmine-Stemmed Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Red Legs', a selection by Massachusetts plantsman Leo Blanchette, carries the largest leaves of any red-stemmed Polygonatum odoratum cultivar on bright carmine-red stalks, distinct from the similarly red-stemmed 'Ruby Slippers' (also sold as 'Red Stem').

directions: Red Legs is a little-known but standout red-stemmed selection of fragrant Solomon's seal, its bright carmine-red, 20-inch stalks set with green leaves that mature to 6 inches long, the largest foliage recorded among the red-stemmed odoratum selections. Scented, tubular, white flowers tipped in green dangle from the leaf axils in spring, followed later by dark berries. It grows a bit more tightly and slightly smaller than typical straight-species Polygonatum odoratum, making it well suited to smaller woodland plantings where the colorful stems can be appreciated up close. Grow in evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and divide clumps in spring once established.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring into rich, humus-heavy soil that never fully dries; 'Smaragd' ('emerald'), selected by German plantsman Ernst Pagels in 1974, is a semi-dwarf form of R. podophylla whose bronze-tinted spring foliage matures to a bright, deep emerald-green.

directions: Smaragd is a compact, semi-dwarf selection of the duck-foot-leaved Rodgersia podophylla, noticeably shorter than the species and most other podophylla cultivars, making it a useful choice for smaller woodland or bog gardens. Its deeply veined, palmate leaves emerge tinged with bronze on tall petioles before settling into the bright, deep emerald-green color that gives the cultivar its name, with creamy-white astilbe-like flower plumes rising above the foliage in early summer. Site it in a sheltered spot with constant moisture and morning sun for the best foliage color without scorching, and mulch heavily to buffer root temperature through summer. Divide congested clumps only occasionally in early spring, since rodgersias resent frequent disturbance.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring into rich, humus-heavy soil that never fully dries; 'Pagode' is an unusually floriferous Rodgersia podophylla selection whose large palmate leaves are carried in distinct tiers, giving rise to its pagoda-like common name.

directions: Pagode forms a full, round plant with large, serrated, palmate leaves held in tiers that create a distinctly layered, pagoda-like silhouette, emerging coppery-bronze in spring, maturing to olive-green through summer, and turning a striking ruby-red in fall. It is one of the most floriferous podophylla selections, topped from late spring into early summer with a great inflorescence of large, creamy-white astilbe-like panicles that rise well above the foliage. Deer generally leave it alone. Site in humus-rich, constantly moist to wet soil in partial shade or gentle morning sun along a pond edge or stream bank, and mulch well to protect the large leaves from scorching in dry spells.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in deep, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; 'Parasol', a hybrid between R. aesculifolia and R. podophylla bred by Eric Smith and Jim Archibald at The Plantsman nursery, combines narrow, serrated, frilly apple-green leaves with tall, columnar creamy-white flower spikes.

directions: Parasol is a hybrid rodgersia combining traits of both its parents: leaflets shaped like R. podophylla's but proportionally longer and narrower, giving the foliage an almost frilly, deeply serrated texture, with tips that take on red tones through summer over a lighter, apple-green base color than many rodgersias. In early to midsummer it sends up tall, columnar spikes of creamy-white flowers well above the foliage on stems that can reach five feet, with an eventual spread to match. Give it deep, fertile, consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade along a pond edge or stream bank, with ample room to reach its full imposing size, and mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; 'Sommergold' (also sold as 'Sungold') is a green-leaved Ligularia dentata selection with erect purple stems carrying bunched heads of bright yellow, strap-petalled daisy flowers.

directions: Unlike the many dark-purple-leaved Ligularia dentata cultivars, Sommergold keeps plain, glossy green, rounded, coarsely toothed foliage, letting its bright yellow, strap-petalled, daisy-like flowers take center stage as they cluster atop erect, contrasting purple stems from mid-summer into autumn. It offers the same bold, tropical-looking leaf texture as its dark-leaved relatives while adding a cheerful pop of clear yellow bloom color, and works well as a foil planted among darker-leaved companions. Grow in cool, evenly moist to boggy, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, since like all bigleaf ligularias it wilts visibly within hours of drying out. Divide congested clumps in spring every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: King Kong Ligularia (Giant Glossy Black-Purple Bigleaf Ligularia)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; 'King Kong' (PP 29,461), a Ligularia dentata x hessei hybrid discovered as a seedling from a 'Britt-Marie Crawford' isolation block in Michigan, carries the same near-black foliage as its parent but with leaves nearly twice as large.

directions: King Kong is a giant-leaved evolution of the popular 'Britt-Marie Crawford', its glossy, black-purple new leaves mellowing to burgundy-purple and reaching up to 16 inches across, roughly twice the leaf size of its parent, giving an even bolder tropical presence in the shade border. In midsummer it sends up branched, greyed-purple panicles topped with dense clusters of large, upright, golden-orange daisy flowers that rise well above the foliage. As with all dark-leaved bigleaf ligularias, grow it in cool, consistently moist to boggy, humus-rich soil in partial shade, protected from hot afternoon sun, since it will wilt dramatically if allowed to dry out even briefly. Divide crowded clumps in spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, consistently moist to boggy, well-drained soil in partial shade; this vigorous hybrid between Ligularia dentata and L. japonica (long grown and sold as L. x palmatiloba) bears deeply cut, toothy, palmate leaves that give it a bold, exotic texture distinct from either parent.

directions: Palmatiloba is a large, vigorous species hybrid combining the rounded boldness of Ligularia dentata with the deeply lobed, lacy texture of L. japonica, producing dramatic, deeply cut palmate leaves up to 10 inches long on a bushy, tussock-forming plant. In mid- to late summer it carries large, orangey-yellow, daisy-like flowers in bunched, flat-topped umbels well above the foliage, creating an exotic, dramatic accent unlike almost anything else in the shade border. Like all ligularias it needs a consistently moist, ideally boggy site in partial shade and will wilt and sulk if allowed to dry out, especially in hot afternoon sun. Give it ample room to reach its full five-foot-plus height and spread, and divide congested clumps in spring.

common_name: Zebra Stripes Evergreen Solomon's Seal (Variegated Evergreen Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in bright shade to full shade; bred by plantsman Hans Hansen, 'Zebra Stripes' was the first named variegated selection of this evergreen Solomon's-seal relative, with gold-and-green banded foliage.

directions: Zebra Stripes is the first named variegated form of Chinese evergreen Solomon's seal, its glossy leaves marked with bold longitudinal bands of gold against green, an effect distinctive enough among evergreen woodland groundcovers to have earned the cultivar its common name. Small, dangling, white, bell-shaped flowers appear beneath the arching foliage in spring, and the striped leaves persist through winter in milder zones, unlike deciduous Polygonatum. It forms a slowly spreading clump via creeping rhizomes and has proven resistant to the sawfly larvae that sometimes disfigure true Solomon's seal. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in bright to full shade, and divide congested clumps in spring to increase the planting.

common_name: Little Hulk Evergreen Solomon's Seal (Extra-Vigorous Giant Evergreen Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in bright shade to full shade; 'Little Hulk', a 2022 Juniper Level Botanic Garden/Plant Delights introduction, is a notably large and vigorous evergreen form that spreads into wide patches over time.

directions: Little Hulk is an ironically named cultivar given its considerable vigor: glossy, evergreen, lance-shaped foliage on 2-foot stems forms a dense colony that can spread to 8 feet wide or more over two decades, making it among the most robust selections of this Chinese evergreen Solomon's-seal relative. Small, fragrant, pendulous white flowers dangle beneath the arching stems in mid-spring, followed by dark berries. Its evergreen foliage persists through winter in milder zones, offering year-round structure that deciduous Polygonatum cannot match. Plant rhizome divisions in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in bright to full shade, and give it room to spread into a substantial groundcover patch in a woodland setting.
